strengths: Addresses a well-motivated and practically important problem: hallucination of library dependencies in LLM-based statement autoformalization, with a clear illustrative failure case (Figure 1a).
The generation-plus-verification paradigm (DDR) is a sensible departure from embedding-based retrieval, avoiding the need for a pre-specified top-k and sidestepping encoder training issues.

The suffix-array verification mechanism is algorithmically sound, with correct complexity analysis (O(N) construction, O(log N) query), and is shown to meaningfully speed up large-scale dependency extraction (2.5 days -> under 2 hours), enabling construction of a 500k-sample dataset.

Reasonably comprehensive experimental design: retrieval-only comparisons (Table 2) as well as downstream autoformalization comparisons (Table 3) across multiple difficulty bins, several strong ICL baselines (GPT-4o, Claude-3.5-Sonnet, DeepSeek-R1, Qwen2.5-Max), and multi-attempt reliability/efficiency analyses (Figures 4-5).
Uses an established, human-aligned semantic equivalence metric (BEq) from prior work rather than relying solely on weaker surface metrics.
Dataset and methodology are stated to be open-sourced and are described as generalizable to other formal corpora/provers, which if realized would benefit the community.
weaknesses: A major confound: the DDR model is built on Qwen3-32B while the RA/R@k baselines are built on the much smaller InternLM2-Math-Base-7B. Because the comparison changes both the retrieval method and the base model simultaneously, it is impossible to attribute the reported gains cleanly to the DDR method itself rather than to base-model capacity; a controlled ablation with matched base models for DDR vs. R@k is needed.

The R@5/R@10 embedding baseline achieves suspiciously low precision/recall (e.g., 0.02-0.13), which is far weaker than typically reported for dense retrieval systems in this space; the paper does not sufficiently investigate or justify why the baseline is this weak (e.g., embedding model choice, indexing granularity), leaving open whether the baseline is a fair, well-tuned point of comparison.

Test sets are small (200 samples per difficulty bin, 5 bins total = 1000 test items) and no variance/significance testing is reported for Table 3 differences, despite the paper itself emphasizing multi-attempt stability elsewhere; some reported gains (e.g., Diff45 BEq 0.59 vs 0.54) are numerically modest and could plausibly fall within noise.

Method and dataset construction are validated only on Lean4/Mathlib via FineLeanCorpus; claims about generalizability to "other formal corpora" and other theorem provers (Coq, Isabelle) are asserted but not empirically tested.

The paper omits comparison to more recent/relevant dependency-retrieval work referenced in its own related work section (e.g., ARIA, Wang et al. 2025b), which limits the completeness of the empirical positioning against the current state of the art.

Some presentation/reproducibility gaps: the open-source dataset link is blank in the manuscript, one in-text citation is empty/missing (page 2, "identifiers and construction of syntax ()"), and the DDR hallucination/failure rate after verification is not explicitly quantified in the main text.

The paper's own Discussion section acknowledges DDR loses compatibility with full retrieval metadata (documentation, usage) required by the baseline autoformalizer framework, and metadata fields were simply set to None for baselines during evaluation — this ad hoc handling could bias the downstream comparison in Table 3 in DDR's favor since the baseline's expected information pipeline is degraded.
Minor writing/grammar issues throughout (e.g., "three direction," "Similiar," "an highly efficient method," "tositives") suggest the manuscript would benefit from a careful proofreading pass.

strengths: Addresses a well-motivated problem (hallucination in formal dependency retrieval for autoformalization) with a simple, efficient generate-then-verify paradigm.

The Suffix Array Check (SAC) mechanism has favorable theoretical complexity (O(sM log N)) and is reused effectively for three purposes: dataset construction, inference-time verification, and downstream analyses (hallucination quantification, difficulty estimation).

Comprehensive experiments spanning five ICL LLMs (Claude, DeepSeek-R1, GPT-4o, Ling-flash, Qwen-Max) and an SFT baseline (RA), across five difficulty-stratified test sets, showing consistent improvements in both retrieval precision/recall and downstream autoformalization metrics (TypeC, BEq).
Useful quantitative framing of ICL hallucination rates (Table 2), which is a novel and interesting analysis not previously reported in this explicit form.

Large-scale (500k+) dependency retrieval dataset construction methodology is described as generalizable to other formal corpora, and the training/inference pipeline (SFT + SAC filtering) is reasonably reproducible given the appendix details on hyperparameters and prompts.
weaknesses: The dataset release link is left blank in the text ("has been made open-access at" with no URL), undermining a central reproducibility claim.

The core technical novelty is modest: SAC is essentially an application of known suffix-array/n-gram matching techniques (cited from Liu et al. 2024) to a lookup task, and DDR is a fairly direct SFT-based generate-then-filter approach; the conceptual contribution is more engineering integration than a new method.

The evaluation protocol for retrieval precision/recall uses a lenient substring/sublist matching criterion (Appendix C) between generated and ground-truth identifiers, which could differentially favor DDR's abbreviated outputs and makes the large precision/recall gap over baselines harder to interpret at face value.

The R@5/R@10 baseline (Liu et al. 2025b) precision figures reported here (0.02-0.10) seem unusually low relative to what one would expect from an embedding-based retriever, raising questions about whether the baseline was faithfully reproduced/tuned, which affects the fairness of the primary comparison.

The RA+DDR integration explicitly suffers from a "format mismatch" with the prior RA framework (abbreviated names vs. full metadata), acknowledged in Limitations, which weakens the claim that DDR is a fully plug-and-play, generalizable module.
No experiments beyond Lean4/Mathlib despite claims of general applicability to other formal corpora (Coq, Isabelle); the generalization claim is untested.

The proposed Depend Rate/Depend Length difficulty metrics are only qualitatively compared against LLM-assigned difficulty labels for a handful of difficulty bins, without a rigorous validation against human judgments or ground truth.
Writing quality has minor grammatical issues and some presentation gaps (e.g., truncated corpus citation list, awkward phrasing) that slightly reduce clarity.
